item.title: Rootshús - Ground is Broken, Voices Rise in Celebration — Icelandic Roots
item.description: Becky Byerly-Adams and Rob Olason The Deuce of August 2026 festivities in Mountain, North Dakota were host to a unique experience. The Groundbreakding for Rootshús by Becky Byerly-Adams August 1 was a beautiful, sunny day; perfect weather for the groundbreaking ceremony for the Icelandic Rootshús in Mountain, North Dakota. item.title: Manitoba Settlements: Argyle and Swan River — Icelandic Roots
item.description: By Sharron Arksey Icelandic settlements spread outside beyond the area of New Iceland over the course of time. Many continued north and west. This article looks at two other areas of Manitoba. Argyle, where the early settlers felt they had arrived in Paradise and yet some of them left, and Swan River. Sharron explores the early days for the settlers, their communities and how they have evolved. ARGYLE There is a story about an Icelandic immigrant who, in 1880, travelled from Gimli to what is...

item.title: In Search of the Lost Children — Icelandic Roots
item.description: By Becky Byerly-Adams [Condensed for Rætur Fréttir/Roots News] As we learn about our heritage, the connection to our ancestors strengthens. It intensifies when opportunities exist to see where they once lived, stand where they stood, walk where they walked. The ultimate connection is finding their eternal place of rest. Growing up in non-Icelandic communities in the United States, long after my Iceland-born grandmother had passed, I was proud of my heritage. Yet I knew little more than a few...

item.title: Book Review: Be Still the Water — Icelandic Roots
item.description: By Brian Borgford Historical Fiction with an Emotional Connection: Comparisons and Contrasts Be Still the Water by Karen Emilson has something for everyone. It takes you through a full range of emotions over the first three quarters of the twentieth century: joy, sadness, grief, anger, love, hope, despair, acceptance, atonement, fear, trust, and acceptance. item.title: Kvennahlaup 2026 — Icelandic Canadian Frón
item.description: The Icelandic Canadian Fron is preparing to host its annual Kvennahlaup—known in English as the Women’s Walk—on Saturday, September 12 at Assiniboine Park. Traditionally held in June, organizers have shifted the event to September in hopes of attracting a wider range of participants. The walk begins at 10 a.m. at the Assiniboine Park Duck Pond, … Continue reading Kvennahlaup 2026

item.title: Icelandic language class fall session — Icelandic Canadian Frón
item.description: The Icelandic Canadian Frón will be offering Icelandic classes again this fall. They will take place at the Scandinavian Cultural Centre, 764 Erin Street. We are planning for 3 classes. Beginners, conversation and grammar. Classes begin September 22, 6:30 p.m. at the Scandinavian Centre. 764 Erin Street. To register online, click the button below.

item.title: Icelandic Festival Events - Summer 2026 — Icelandic Roots
item.description: by Doreen Borgfjord McFarlane Each summer for many years, Icelandic festivals take place in various communities in North America. Two of the main festivals, in Mountain and Gimli, occur on the long weekend in August. Celebrations with songs, dancing, food and parades, as well as numerous other events are shared. Some festival-goers attend both locations. This year Doreen, accompanied by her husband Eigil, did just that. And, what a time they had... You may call yourself an Icelandic-American...

item.title: Haraldur Bessason: August’s Interesting Icelander — Icelandic Roots
item.description: By Sharron Arksey Photo Credit: Winnipeg Free Press1 If you are a Manitoban of Icelandic descent, you likely recognize the name Haraldur Bessason (I155214). As the Chair of the Icelandic Department at the University of Manitoba for several decades and a former editor of Lögberg-Heimskringla, he was a well-known figure in western Icelandic circles. But I did not know that Bessason was born in Iceland, nor that his remains are buried there. I was surprised last year to see his grave in the...

item.title: Road Trip: The West Side of Lake Manitoba — Icelandic Roots
item.description: By Sharron Arksey Photo Credit: The author. Manitoba’s Provincial Trunk Highway 50 begins where it meets the Yellowhead Highway (Provincial Trunk Highway Number16) in the south-central portion of the province. The paved highway stretches north for approximately 50 miles before it makes a turn to the west, ending at McCreary, MB. Its north-south route parallels the western shore of Lake Manitoba.
